{"id": "4:49/q01", "question": "What does أَلَمْ تَرَ convey here?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is explained as epistemic perception or as a summons to wonder at the claim.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q01/p1", "position": "It calls on the Prophet to know or be informed of their case, rather than literally see it.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda (MAJAZ) denies literal eyesight; al-Zajjaj's language scholars say the question conveys information and commands knowledge of their story; Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj give the informed and known glosses; al-Tabari makes this perception of the heart; Tabrisi combines both glosses. Jishumi and Tabrisi distinguish looking or turning attention from achieved perception, including bodily, mental, merciful, hostile, expectant and disputational uses; Tabrisi says God may be called seeing but not looking."}, {"id": "4:49/q01/p2", "position": "It directs attention to their conduct and expresses astonishment at their claim.", "reasons": "Muqatil says to look at their action; al-Nahhas and Bursevi stress the Prophet's amazement, the latter despite their disbelief and grave sins; al-Alusi gives either their purity claim or supposed daily erasure of sins as the object of wonder."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q02", "question": "Is there a variant reading of أَلَمْ تَرَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q02/p1", "position": "Al-Sulami reads the rāʾ still after loss of the jussive letter.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi says this reading of alam tarh occurs throughout the Quran, illustrates the dialect's added sukūn with an anonymous poem about divine guidance and misguidance; Jishumi calls the open form more elevated."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q03", "question": "Who are ٱلَّذِينَ يُزَكُّونَ أَنفُسَهُم?", "turns_on": "Whether contextual reports restrict the referent to Jews, include Christians or the People of the Book, or allow the general wording to reach later self-praisers.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q03/p1", "position": "Jews, particularly those making claims of purity and special status.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Bahri ibn Amr and Marhab ibn Zayd; the majority according to Abu Hayyan, and all interpreters according to Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi, identify Jews. Tabatabai prefers Jews or some of them in context and cites 5:18, 2:80, 62:6. Ibn Ashur points to claims in 5:18 and 2:111. Study Quran specifies some Madinan Jews as a reported narrower identification."}, {"id": "4:49/q03/p2", "position": "Jews and Christians, or the People of the Book generally.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan cites the claims of divine sonship, love and exclusive Paradise (5:18, 2:111); Ibn Zayd includes both groups' claims of obedience. Ibn Jurayj applies the children's prayer account to both. Bagha wi also attributes this to al-Dahhak, Qatada and Muqatil; Tabrisi adds a report from al-Baqir. Study Quran prefers the wider People of the Book reference over Madinan Jews. Biqai includes claims of guidance, brief fire, unearned praise and others following their desires (2:80, 2:111, 3:188, 4:27)."}, {"id": "4:49/q03/p3", "position": "The rebuke extends to anyone who claims purity or exceptional piety.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, Alusi and Study Quran apply the general wording beyond the initial community; Asad includes Jews and Christians under deeper shirk and also Muslims who venerate saints as divine."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q04", "question": "What did their self-purification consist of?", "turns_on": "The rival reports identify different purity claims and acts; Tabari questions proof for the prayer account, Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi question its fit, and Qurtubi favors mutual praise.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q04/p1", "position": "They claimed divine sonship and love, exclusive Paradise, election, or privileged exemption from punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan cites 5:18 and 2:111; Ibn Zayd adds claimed obedience. Razi adds brief punishment (2:80) and ancestral intercession; Biqai adds unearned praise and demands that believers follow their desires (3:188, 4:27); Tabatabai adds chosen friendship (62:6), and Kuranyolu says such praise confers no status. Asad adds Christian reliance on Jesus' vicarious atonement."}, {"id": "4:49/q04/p2", "position": "They declared themselves sinless, including the claim that daytime and nighttime sins were alternately forgiven.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak likens them to newborns, while Ibn Abi Hatim reports a variant likening them to sinless ancestors; al-Suddi says boys learned Torah young and that adults' daytime sins were erased at night. Study Quran observes that the Quran does not explicitly attest these reported claims."}, {"id": "4:49/q04/p3", "position": "They put children forward as prayer leaders, relying on the children's alleged innocence to cleanse the adults.", "reasons": "Mujahid speaks of children leading prayer; Ibn Jurayj adds supplication and extends the group to Christians; Ibn Abbas adds offerings or sacrifices; Abu Hayyan says the adult worshipers sought forgiveness behind them. Tabari finds no authoritative report establishing this account; Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi call it remote from the verse's aim. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas reject the premise that another innocent person purifies a sinner."}, {"id": "4:49/q04/p4", "position": "They claimed dead children or forebears would intercede with God and purify them.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas' reports variously say deceased children or ancestors, and call the children a means of nearness to God; Razi mentions prophetic forebears. Study Quran records mutual absolution through intercession as an additional variant."}, {"id": "4:49/q04/p5", "position": "They praised, vouched for, or declared one another pure, sometimes for worldly advantage.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud's account concerns mutual praise; Mawardi specifies Jews seeking worldly gain; the man in Abdullah's report flatters someone unable to help or harm him, loses religion or incurs God's anger, and gains nothing. Qurtubi prefers this as the apparent meaning."}, {"id": "4:49/q04/p6", "position": "They verbally certified their own deeds, piety, obedience or nearness to God.", "reasons": "Tabrisi gives the direct declaration 'we are pure'; Razi compares testimony to a witness's uprightness. Ibn Atiyya says words cannot confer the purity established by good deeds and God; generalizing authors include anyone making such claims."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q05", "question": "What happened when Jews brought children to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Different narrated occasions and their named actors; Tabari disputes sufficient transmission for the prayer account.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q05/p1", "position": "Jewish men asked whether their children had sins and, after the Prophet said no, claimed their own sins were erased day and night.", "reasons": "Names vary: Muqatil has Bahri ibn Amr and Marhab ibn Zayd; Baghawi adds al-Numan ibn Awfa; Ibn Jawzi has Bahri ibn Awn; Abu Hayyan has Bahri ibn Amr and Marhab. Farra, Kalbi, Ibn Abbas and others report the alternation of day and night erasure; the reports say the verse answered their claim. Study Quran notes the Quran itself does not explicitly attest these details."}, {"id": "4:49/q05/p2", "position": "Some report that Jews made sinless children lead worship or give offerings, prompting revelation.", "reasons": "Mujahid reports prayer leadership; Ibn Abbas adds offerings; Ikrima specifies prepubescent boys. Abu Malik and others explicitly call it the occasion of revelation."}, {"id": "4:49/q05/p3", "position": "Another report connects the passage with a Jewish delegation's alliance with Quraysh and Kaʿb's judgment in favor of idolatry.", "reasons": "Elmalılı names Huyay ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn Ashraf with seventy Jewish horsemen, their journey to Mecca to break a pact, Quraysh's demand that they prostrate to idols, their compliance, and Abu Sufyan's question after hearing Muhammad's monotheist call; Ka'b commended Quraysh's services and preferred them to the believers."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q06", "question": "What does يُزَكُّونَ mean, and what is its root sense?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q06/p1", "position": "It is purifying or declaring someone pure and free of faults or sins; its root also means sound growth or increase in goodness.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj, Ibn Jawzi and Tabrisi connect zakā to growth; Tabrisi uses sound crops; al-Raghib says growth by God's blessing. Jishumi says description itself can count as tazkiya; Baydawi and Alusi stress removing blameworthy conduct or speech, with 91:9 and 9:103; Damghani gives vindication or acquittal (2:174, 18:74). Kuranyolu distinguishes character improvement and moral education through acts from speech attesting honesty or freedom from grave faults; al-Raghib gives the same deed and speech distinction (87:14, 53:32)."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q07", "question": "Why does the verse say أَنفُسَهُم in the plural for mutual praise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q07/p1", "position": "Members of one religion count as one self, so their praising one another is called praising themselves.", "reasons": "Tabrisi explains the shared religious identity behind the plural."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q08", "question": "What does the verse teach about praising oneself or another person?", "turns_on": "Whether praise is truthful and useful, whether it claims knowledge of the inward state, and whether any human virtue is treated as independent of God.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q08/p1", "position": "Verbal self-praise, self-certification and vanity are condemned; real standing belongs to God and good deeds.", "reasons": "Qurtubi joins 53:32 and notes the renaming of Barrah as Zaynab in Muslim; Egyptian titles implying purity can mask vice. Ibn Kathir reports Umar warning that declaring oneself a believer, learned or Paradise-bound reveals the opposite, and that self-admiration is feared. Joseph refuses to acquit his soul (12:53). Sulami and Sufis say the carnal soul is unfit as a sit

God's spoken praise of the prophets, listed by Tabatabai with verses for Adam, Noah, Abraham, Idris, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Jesus, Solomon, Job and Muhammad, is authoritative."}, {"id": "4:49/q08/p4", "position": "Practical purification by good deeds and moral improvement is encouraged, while boasting of it is forbidden.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib distinguishes acts that show virtue from speech that claims it (87:14, 53:32); Kuranyolu describes moral education and escape from bad traits; Tabatabai says acknowledging real learning and honoring scholars follows truth (22:32, 39:9), though scholars must not boast."}, {"id": "4:49/q08/p5", "position": "Self-reliance is counted a virtue by some researchers.", "reasons": "Tabatabai attributes this view to fellow researchers following Maghrebi thinkers; he rejects it, citing Quranic dependence on God and deriving strength and honor from Him (3:173, 2:165, 10:65)."}, {"id": "4:49/q08/p6", "position": "Reliance on God, rather than independent self-reliance, is the virtue.", "reasons": "Tabatabai invokes 3:173, 2:165 and 10:65; people cannot own virtue independently because God owns their possessions."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q09", "question": "How does بَلِ correct the self-praisers?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding denial is understood directly from bal or supplied as an omitted clause.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q09/p1", "position": "It turns from and repudiates their claim, making God's purification the only effective certification.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says they are unqualified to certify themselves; Ibn Ashur says bal must expressly repudiate them, for without it they might still expect inclusion among those God purifies. Alusi says the correction concerns their false self-purification, not miserliness and envy."}, {"id": "4:49/q09/p2", "position": "It is joined to an implicit statement that they err or cannot truly purify themselves.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa reconstructs 'they erred; rather, God purifies'; Alusi supplies 'they do not truly purify themselves' before bal."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q10", "question": "What does God's يُزَكِّى مَن يَشَآءُ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether purification here denotes moral cleansing, God's true testimony, acceptance of deeds, creation of faith, or inward transformation.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q10/p1", "position": "God cleanses from sin, reforms and makes pure whom He wills, enabling obedience.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls it reform; Tabari specifies divine enabling to abandon disobedience and obey, rather than effective self-praise; Thalabi, Zajjaj, Baghawi and Tabrisi stress cleansing, acquittal and setting right. Wahidi identifies monotheists and increase in righteousness; Ibn Kathir says God alone knows hidden realities. Biqai adds divine knowledge, power, wisdom and justice and created qualities producing righteous acts."}, {"id": "4:49/q10/p2", "position": "God judges, attests to and verbally describes as pure those He knows and approves.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi and Abu Hayyan ground this in God's knowledge of hidden virtue; Razi says only God knows inward piety (53:32). Tabatabai distinguishes practical favor from verbal testimony and says verbal praise is meant here; he lists God's praise of named prophets. Ibn Ashur calls it God's testimony in place of self-certification."}, {"id": "4:49/q10/p3", "position": "God accepts a person's deeds, thereby purifying that person.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports this alternative and says God does not so purify the Jews but punishes them."}, {"id": "4:49/q10/p4", "position": "God creates believers' faith, the highest form of purification.", "reasons": "Razi argues from faith's rank as the greatest and noblest purification and God's choice of whom to purify."}, {"id": "4:49/q10/p5", "position": "In an inward reading, God replaces the ego's transient qualities with His own enduring attributes.", "reasons": "Qashani says inherent ego qualities cannot purify themselves and invokes 59:9 on greed; a Prophetic saying about resurrection overtaking the living depicts one who learns tawhid before the ego dies by annihilation, then becomes a libertine heretic. God erases ego qualities and grants lasting divine attributes without withholding their due."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q11", "question": "What does وَلَا يُظْلَمُونَ فَتِيلًا assure?", "turns_on": "Which people the pronoun covers and whether the promise is applied to punishment, reward, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q11/p1", "position": "God wrongs no one by even the least amount, withholding no due good or imposing no undeserved evil.", "reasons": "Tabari includes both allocation of purification and rights, while affirming that He grants success or leaves the disobedient in failure by choice. Muqatil and Wahidi stress no loss of deeds or reward; Ibn Abbas in Durr includes both good and evil. Tabrisi, Biqai and Abu Hayyan reason that if no tiny injustice occurs, none greater occurs, comparing 4:40; Ibn Qutayba compares naqir. Bursevi defines wrong as extra punishment or reduced reward; Ibn Ashur says God knows deserts and guides truly. Bint Shati says all three Quranic occurrences concern God's reckoning."}, {"id": "4:49/q11/p2", "position": "The self-praisers receive exactly the punishment or blame earned by their false claim.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi and Nasafi give this as one reading; Tabrisi, Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi apply it to their punishment. Alusi prefers this warning-context reading and joins the clause to an implied statement that they will be punished."}, {"id": "4:49/q11/p3", "position": "Those God purifies receive the entire reward of their purity or obedience.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi and Nasafi offer this alternative, Razi comparing 4:40; Sam in says they lose none of their purification; Alusi calls it a circumstantial reading referring to the Resurrection."}, {"id": "4:49/q11/p4", "position": "Both the self-praisers' just punishment and the divinely purified people's reward are fully measured.", "reasons": "Samin reports this two-group reading; Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya include both antecedents; Abu al-Baqa allows it with an independent sentence, and Alusi reports it but prefers the warning reading."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q12", "question": "To whom does the pronoun in يُظْلَمُونَ refer?", "turns_on": "The nearest grammatical antecedent versus the warning context and an inclusive reading of both groups.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q12/p1", "position": "The preceding self-praisers.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Samin and Abu Hayyan allow this; Alusi prefers it in the warning context, and connects the clause with an omitted statement of their punishment. Bursevi and Baydawi likewise speak of the claimants' punishment."}, {"id": "4:49/q12/p2", "position": "Those whom God chooses to purify.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin prefer the nearest antecedent man yasha, with Abu Hayyan noting the reference can follow sense; Samin says bal begins a disconnected correction. Alusi says they obtain full reward."}, {"id": "4:49/q12/p3", "position": "Both the claimants and those God purifies.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi say justice toward others is known independently; Samin reports the two-group reading and Abu al-Baqa's independent-clause account, while allowing the antecedent also with a circumstantial clause; Alusi reports but does not prefer it."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q13", "question": "How is وَلَا يُظْلَمُونَ attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause describes the preceding action's circumstance or starts a new assertion, with a possible implied antecedent statement.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q13/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause related to what precedes.", "reasons": "Samin allows this, including with both groups as antecedent; Alusi gives a circumstantial reading for those God purifies, who receive their full reward."}, {"id": "4:49/q13/p2", "position": "It is an independent sentence, possibly connected to an omitted statement of punishment.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa assigns both groups as referent in an independent clause; Alusi attaches it to an omitted statement that their heinous claim will receive just punishment."}]}

{"id": "4:49/q15", "question": "What physical thing is فَتِيلًا?", "turns_on": "Which tiny object supplies the image; several sources treat the alternatives as equivalent evidence for negligible amount.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q15/p1", "position": "The minute fiber or thread in a date stone's groove or cleft.", "reasons": "This is attributed to Ibn Abbas, Ata, Mujahid, Qatada, Dahhak, Hasan and others by multiple collectors. Some call it the groove itself, a line inside the stone or the thread on its back where the palm sprouts; Ibn Kathir says the alternatives are close. Authors distinguish naqir as a back dimple or dot and qitmir as husk, skin or wrapping; Mujahid also compares an egg membrane and reed skin. Samin lists thafruq as a fourth minute date-stone object, the first three appearing in scripture. Ibn Qutayba says these images are figurative for minute justice; Study Quran links 4:77, 4:124, 17:71 and 19:60."}, {"id": "4:49/q15/p2", "position": "The minute dirt, lint or fuzz rolled off rubbing fingers or palms.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Abu Malik and Suddi transmit this; Ibn Abi Hatim also cites Mujahid and Said ibn Jubayr. Abu Hayyan cites al-Azhari on the parallel date-stone images and matching verse endings."}]}

{"id": "4:49/q17", "question": "What is the accusative function of فَتِيلًا?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative is governed as an object, a specification of amount, or an implicit absolute object.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q17/p1", "position": "It is the second object of 'wrong,' the first having become the passive subject.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya states this; Ali ibn Isa is cited by Tabrisi and Alusi; Samin explains the passive promotion."}, {"id": "4:49/q17/p2", "position": "It is an accusative of specification or a measure standing for 'a fatil's amount.'", "reasons": "Jishumi describes the measured object and an alternative specification; Ali ibn Isa permits specification, compared by Alusi to 'I sweated sweat.'"}, {"id": "4:49/q17/p3", "position": "It substitutes for an absolute object of injustice, or modifies an omitted verbal noun.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the comparison particle is omitted and compares 4:40; Samin supplies the omitted verbal noun and likewise compares 4:40; Samarrai says the expression conveys both physical thread and smallest injustice."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q18", "question": "How does this verse connect with its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize different links in the passage: the preceding sins, the following accusation, or Quranic parallels.", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q18/p1", "position": "It rebukes the People of the Book after discussion of unbelief, shirk and scriptural distortion, and their self-praise helps explain the following charge of lying.", "reasons": "Tabrisi places it after unbelief and distortion; Razi places the privileged-status claims after the shirk threat of 4:48; Tabatabai sees Jewish arrogance, refusal to believe and the divine curse as consequences of self-admiration. Wahidi and Tabari connect 4:50 to the falsehood. {"id": "4:49/q20", "question": "Can an innocent child purify a sinner?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q20/p1", "position": "No; a sinner is not purified through another person's innocence.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives this answer to the claim concerning sinless children; Ibn Kathir rejects that claim on the same ground."}]}
{"id": "4:49/q21", "question": "Who is Maʿbad in Ibn Kathir's report?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:49/q21/p1", "position": "Maʿbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUwaym, a Basran Qadari.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir supplies this identification for the person named in his report discussion."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q01", "question": "Who are the disbelievers threatened here?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding discussion restricts the address or introduces a general threat.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q01/p1", "position": "The warning covers all disbelievers, including rejecters of Muhammad or any prophet.", "reasons": "Tabari includes Jews of Israel and other persistent deniers; Ibn Atiyya extends the warning from rebellious Israelites to all who share their unbelief; Ibn Ashur calls it broader than the preceding passage."}, {"id": "4:56/q01/p2", "position": "They are the Jews.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies them as Jews."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q02", "question": "What constitutes disbelief in the signs?", "turns_on": "The outward acts of rejecting evidence versus an inward veil.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q02/p1", "position": "It includes denial, neglect, doubt, and knowing rejection.", "reasons": "Razi lists denying evidentiary status, neglecting consideration, raising doubts, and obstinacy or envy despite knowledge, referring to 2:6; Biqai says deniers conceal what intellect disclosed."}, {"id": "4:56/q02/p2", "position": "It is being veiled from divine manifestations.", "reasons": "Qashani connects this veil to God's attributes and acts."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q03", "question": "What are God's signs here?", "turns_on": "Whether signs means scripture specifically, all proofs, or divine manifestations.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q03/p1", "position": "They are divine proofs, including revelation and prophetic signs.", "reasons": "Tabari emphasizes revealed proofs of Muhammad's truth; Tabrisi includes oneness and the Prophet; Razi includes signs of God's essence, acts, attributes and names, plus angels, books and messengers; Bursevi includes Quran and miracles."}, {"id": "4:56/q03/p2", "position": "They are the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies the Qur'an."}, {"id": "4:56/q03/p3", "position": "They are God's manifestations in attributes and acts.", "reasons": "Qashani relates them to knowledge, wisdom and sovereignty in Abraham's household."}]}

{"id": "4:56/q06", "question": "How is nuslihim read?", "turns_on": "Vocalization of initial nun and pronoun suffix.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q06/p1", "position": "Humayd reads with fatha on initial nun, from triliteral salaya, meaning roast.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Samin report it; Ibn Atiyya cites the roasted sheep hadith; Tha'labi also gives a gloss of putting into fire."}, {"id": "4:56/q06/p2", "position": "The common reading has damma on initial nun, from asla.", "reasons": "Jishumi says aslaytuhu means cast into fire; Ibn Atiyya says bring near and cast in, equivalent to doubled sallaytu; Ibn Ashur derives it from if'al. {"id": "4:56/q07", "question": "What does nuslihim naran mean?", "turns_on": "The verb's causative admission and roasting senses.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q07/p1", "position": "God will cast or admit them into fire.", "reasons": "Tabari says this entails scorching; Tha'labi, Baghawi, Nasafi, Tabrisi, Jishumi and Bursevi explain admission; Ibn Kathir says fire envelops every part. {"id": "4:56/q08", "question": "How is naran governed?", "turns_on": "The governing verb changes with the reading.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q08/p1", "position": "On Humayd's fatha reading, an omitted preposition governs its sense.", "reasons": "Tha'labi understands bi-nar; Jishumi says roast with fire; Qurtubi understands in a fire."}, {"id": "4:56/q08/p2", "position": "On the common reading, naran is a direct object.", "reasons": "Jishumi identifies the object on damma; Ibn Ashur calls it a second object on the pattern of a'ta, citing 2:61."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q09", "question": "Why is fire indefinite?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q09/p1", "position": "Indefiniteness magnifies the fire as formidable.", "reasons": "Alusi presents an immense, dreadful fire."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q10", "question": "How does kullama govern and express repetition?", "turns_on": "Whether ma itself or the full construction gives universality, and where the clause attaches.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q10/p1", "position": "It is a temporal adverb of each occurrence, governed by baddalnahum.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Alusi call it a temporal adverb; Samin makes its clause circumstantial from the object of nuslihim; Abu Hayyan calls ma temporal-source, its clause conditional in force and also relates it to nuslihim. Zarkashi says ma and clause stand for time, with kull accusative as adverb; bare ma is not itself a time adverb. Zarkashi contrasts repeated marriage and divorce with bare kull, citing 2:25."}, {"id": "4:56/q10/p2", "position": "Its repetition arises from temporal ma's own universality, with kull reinforcing it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan's account is reported by Zarkashi, who objects that source ma has no independent universality."}, {"id": "4:56/q10/p3", "position": "Its repetition arises from the whole kullama construction.", "reasons": "Zarkashi rejects assigning generality to ma alone; some legal theorists distinguish intentional generalization of acts with kullama from intentional generalization of nouns with bare kull."}, {"id": "4:56/q10/p4", "position": "The kullama clause qualifies naran.", "reasons": "Samin records this possible analysis with an omitted resumptive pronoun and calls it weak."}]}

{"id": "4:56/q13", "question": "What are the replacement skins?", "turns_on": "Whether ghayraha changes the underlying skin, replaces its material, names clothing, or figuratively depicts duration.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q13/p1", "position": "The very same skin is restored with changed form or quality.", "reasons": "Tabari and Zajjaj compare remaking a ring; Zajjaj adds that resurrection itself recreated decayed skin. Wahidi cites Zajjaj, Ibn Kaysan, Ibn al-Anbari, Farra's ring-to-hoop, Abu al-Abbas's tabdil versus ibdal distinction, and Mubarrad's form-change view supported by Ibn Abbas. {"id": "4:56/q16", "question": "How often are skins consumed or replaced?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted counts and whether a fixed number is asserted.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q16/p1", "position": "Seventy thousand times each day.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Tha'labi, Baghawi, Ibn Jawzi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, Durr and Alusi report al-Hasan; variants count roasting, skin consumption, or flesh consumption; several say the consumed return when commanded."}, {"id": "4:56/q16/p2", "position": "One hundred times in an hour.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim, Tha'labi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Durr transmit Mu'adh's explanation confirmed by Umar as Prophetic; Itqan calls its Tabarani route weak."}, {"id": "4:56/q16/p3", "position": "Seven times each day.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies days measured as worldly days; Kashshaf attributes this to a Prophetic report without grading; Qurtubi reports Muqatil and Abu Hayyan records the figure."}, {"id": "4:56/q16/p4", "position": "Seventy times each day or each cycle.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan attribute seventy replacements to al-Hasan, with white-paper skins; Bursevi reports seventy daily and return on command."}, {"id": "4:56/q16/p5", "position": "One hundred twenty times in an hour.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir, Durr and Alusi give Ka'b's pre-Islamic reading affirmed by Umar as something heard from the Prophet; Alusi gives Ibn Umar's route."}, {"id": "4:56/q16/p6", "position": "The replacement may recur many times in an hour.", "reasons": "Alusi allows this without a fixed figure."}, {"id": "4:56/q16/p7", "position": "The tar garments are replaced a hundred or a hundred thousand times daily.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports the proposal while calling it far-fetched."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q17", "question": "What color or form are the replacement skins?", "turns_on": "Different reported descriptions.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q17/p1", "position": "They are white like sheets of paper.", "reasons": "Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas transmit this comparison through Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Tha'labi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan and Durr; Kashshaf links white skins to al-Hasan's seventy replacements."}, {"id": "4:56/q17/p2", "position": "There are one hundred skins with differently colored torments between each pair.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Yazid al-Hadrami gives this in Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Kathir and Durr."}, {"id": "4:56/q17/p3", "position": "The skin is stretched like a wild ass's hide, with worms between skin, flesh and blood.", "reasons": "Tha'labi reports Mujahid's description."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q18", "question": "What size and bodily features are reported for the damned?", "turns_on": "Different reported measurements and features.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q18/p1", "position": "An earlier book gives skin as forty cubits and a belly able to hold a mountain.", "reasons": "Al-Rabi's versions vary: Tabari gives height seventy cubits; Ibn Abi Hatim gives a ninety-cubit measure for san; Ibn Kathir gives tooth ninety cubits; Durr gives teeth seventy cubits. {"id": "4:56/q19", "question": "How can replacement skin be punished justly?", "turns_on": "Whether the skin is a moral subject and whether identity depends on the same material.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q19/p1", "position": "The continuing person or soul suffers; skin conveys pain but is not the guilty subject.", "reasons": "Tabari says skin and flesh may be insentient; Zajjaj rejects treating skin as sinner; Tha'labi says spirits mediate pain; Mawardi, Wahidi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Alusi, Ibn Ashur and Kuranyolu distinguish person from instrument. {"id": "4:56/q26", "question": "Why does the verse end with God's might and wisdom?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q26/p1", "position": "The names assure execution of a wise and just threat.", "reasons": "Zajjaj answers skeptics by pointing to wisdom in all God's acts; Ibn Atiyya says no rival overcomes God and He judges rightly; Alusi says the clause explains casting into fire and skin renewal, with God's name repeated to ground the ruling; Ibn Ashur relates might to complete punishment and wisdom to its particular form."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q27", "question": "How does this verse connect with its context?", "turns_on": "How the general threat follows the prior discussion.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q27/p1", "position": "It broadens and explains the preceding warning, then sets threat against promised reward.", "reasons": "Tabari directs the warning to Israelite Jews and other persistent unbelievers; Jishumi and Tabrisi say discussion of believers and unbelievers leads to corresponding promise and threat; Ibn Atiyya and Razi say a specific threat expands to all unbelievers; Baydawi calls it confirmation; Abu Hayyan contrasts ensuing believers' reward and cites 3:106; Ibn Ashur calls the verse a set-apart coda."}, {"id": "4:56/q27/p2", "position": "It resonates with other fire and renewal verses.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi cite 17:97's rekindled fire; Wahidi cites 2:162 against a respite; Ibn Ashur recalls 4:10 and 4:30; the skin-as-garment reading invokes 14:49-50."}]}
{"id": "4:56/q28", "question": "What does the passage disclose in an inward reading?", "turns_on": "Different inner referents of fire and skins.", "positions": [{"id": "4:56/q28/p1", "position": "God manifests clarification to the elect.", "reasons": "Sulami reports this gloss."}, {"id": "4:56/q28/p2", "position": "The fire is longing for perfection while the veil persists.", "reasons": "Qashani says nature and capacity demand perfection, but a rooted veil bars it; God's might humiliates through unfulfilled longing."}, {"id": "4:56/q28/p3", "position": "The fire is coercion from God's overpowering attributes.", "reasons": "Qashani says this takes a form suited to their states."}, {"id": "4:56/q28/p4", "position": "The fire is their evil selves craving denied habitual pleasures.", "reasons": "Qashani links deprivation to their own dispositions."}, {"id": "4:56/q28/p5", "position": "Renewed skins are renewed veils of the body.", "reasons": "Qashani says as bodily coverings fall, new veils replace them, prolonging the fires of deprivation; divine wisdom matches what they chose through appetitive and angry impulses."}]}

{"id": "5:90/q03", "question": "Why is wine called khamr?", "turns_on": "The explanations derive the name from its effect on reason, its fermentation, or separation of liquid from sediment.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q03/p1", "position": "It covers or clouds the intellect.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Jishumi, Tabrisi, Razi, Asad and ʿUmar connect the name to covering; Jishumi gives vessels, khimar, crowds, dough, sorrow and concealed testimony as related usage."}, {"id": "5:90/q03/p2", "position": "It is named for being left to ferment and change in smell.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Aʿrabi supplies this etymology in Jishumi and Razi; al-Khalil associates its derivation with fermentation and boiling."}, {"id": "5:90/q03/p3", "position": "It is named for straining the clear liquid from settled sediment.", "reasons": "Saʿid b. al-Musayyib gives this explanation."}]}
